case_data.title: Collaborative AI Governance for Tomorrow's Democracies
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
AI governance for democracy demands a multistakeholder, well-networked framework. This was the finding of our Collaborative AI Governance for Tomorrow’s Democracies project, which consist of three phases - deep issue exploration, participatory engagement, and dissemination and practical implementation. Our approach is collaborative, participatory, and co-creative by design, uniting people with experience, power, and expertise to co-create a framework and insights for systemic change that deliver real impact. What surfaces is a new understanding of what needs to be true to create change, shining a particular spotlight on and giving voice to the lived experience of CSOs across the globe.

The project’s impact was delivered through a systematic review of evidence of the AI governance landscape, furthered through a qualitative study with representatives from civil society, regulatory and public bodies, research institutes and academics, tech companies, and the wider private sector. In all, we consulted more than 50 stakeholders to co-create an approach to increasing citizens' role in governance, understanding and overcoming the barriers to engagement, and exploring effective models for inclusion. 

The outcome of the project is three-fold. Firstly, we delivered a first-of-its-kind framework for collaborative AI governance, which we have called an AI Issue Association, that makes space for effective participation of citizens and civil society. Our findings show that to do this, a strong mandate with enforcement teeth, granular and well-scoped problem definitions, practical commitments, and balanced power dynamics through inclusive, depoliticised structures are all prerequisites. Only when these elements are in place can citizen participation move from consultation to governance. Our project’s second phase - the Power to Shape AI CSO Conversation, co-created a systematised set of needs, barriers, and enablers for civil society to fulfil its role as agenda-setters, wielding effective influence over AI governance. And thirdly, we built and tapped into existing networks of civil society organisations, academics, and AI governing regulatory bodies, to apply the findings in practice. Our ongoing work now focuses on deploying a citizen engagement on the role of AI in hindering and improving democratic processes as well as operationalising the framework through our coalition-building activities.
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b:
The project constitutes a framework intended to provide evidence-based grounding for further action, rather than a completed intervention. Its ultimate impact depends on large-scale coalition-building efforts and on the framework being actively taken forward by partners across sectors. This is a systemic change initiative for a wicked problem with no straightforward solution. In fact, one of the biggest findings of the framework creation phase was the need for people to take radical personal responsibility to influence change in the areas where they hold power. The value demonstrated to date is foundational, laying the groundwork for collective action that has yet to be fully realised at scale.

Sustaining and expanding this work requires dedicated funding and committed partnerships. To address this, we have applied for funding through the EU-funded ScaleDem project for a first-of-its kind citizen participatory engagement on democratic bias in AI in Bulgaria and are pursuing a partnership with Make.org to support a larger-scale engagement effort, alongside broader coalition-building efforts across our expanding partnership network on human-centric AI (50+ partners to date). Direct citizen engagement represents the critical next phase of the project, and securing the funding necessary to deliver it remains an active priority.
case_data.headline-findings:
The current AI governance landscape is dominated by a narrow set of state and corporate actors, even though AI's impacts are whole-of-society by nature and by design. Exacerbating this is the evidence gathered across our stakeholder groups that the impact of consultative processes and grassroots participatory approaches is limited by the absence of common frameworks and tools, transparency and follow-through, and openness to more diverse actors.

AI governance for democracy needs to be a broad-participation and well-networked approach, inclusive of a wide range of participants, like citizens and CSOs, that are currently underrepresented, alongside more “traditional” agents of change, within a model that effectively and actively balances power as a function of its design and mandate. 

A viable governance model that meaningfully incorporates citizen and civil society inputs must have a strong, legally backed mandate, well-framed outcome-oriented issues, practical solutions, modulated power dynamics, and procedural openness and visibility. 

The involvement of citizens in co-regulation, the moderation of private sector behaviour by up and downstream actor influence, and the integration of citizen wisdom are key requirements for generating meaningful change in the way AI is governed in the future.  

Importantly, CSOs’ readiness for participating in AI governance remains low, driven by a self-reinforcing exclusion narrative, discouraging proactive efforts towards the very engagement, capacity-building, and awareness-raising that would earn them a seat at the table. 

Key barriers to effective CSO agenda-setting are: deployment of AI in public services without transparency and accountability; barriers limiting access to information about AI use; ethical risks from poor data governance; perception of civil society as blockers that sidelines deliberation in favour of moving fast; and fragmentation of CSO efforts lacking shared infrastructure to coordinate and strategise together.

Key enablers of more effective CSO engagement include: mass awareness and public mobilisation through simple, relatable narratives at scale; strategic capacity-building to navigate informal decision-making spaces and build alliances; cross-sector coalitions to boost credibility and reach; shift from critique to offering practical alternatives and proven methods; stronger, aligned messaging grounded in lived experience; and early engagement in policy cycles with concrete recommendations.
case_data.additional-acknowledgements: Lidia Velkova, Anna Colom, Marta Poblet, Tim Davies, Dr. Peter Thomond, Jake Hirsch-Allen
case_data.inclusion-efforts: Efforts were made to ensure the recruitment and engagement process was accessible and inclusive. We designed a flexible process that respected participants' other life and professional commitments, recognising that many CSO representatives, academics, and public sector stakeholders operate under significant time constraints. One-on-one interviews were conducted online and scheduled around participants' availability, lowering barriers to entry and removing the need for travel. Online co-creation on our participatory platform, Clever Together Conversations, was asynchronous, allowing participants to contribute at their own leisure. Two virtual workshops were also held to accommodate participants across different time zones. We sought to accommodate individual accessibility needs, adapting the format and approach to ensure that participation was as open and equitable as possible.
case_data.project-title: Collaborative AI Governance for Tomorrow's Democracies
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include:
Questions around the human-centric governance of AI are inseparable from the wider socio-technical polycrisis that defines our current reality. Trust is declining and polarisation is growing. Meanwhile, regulation remains fragmented, abstract, and insufficient to the scale of the challenge. The current approach to AI governance predominantly focuses on states and Big Tech as the two key stakeholder groups afforded leverage and decision-making power. However, AI is a technology that impacts the whole of society. Its implications extend far beyond governments and Big Tech alone.

The initiative advances broad-participation governance frameworks that place citizens and civil society organisations (CSOs) on an equal footing in the AI governance ecosystem. The case for participatory AI rests on both principle and pragmatism. On principle, it stems from a commitment to democracy, human rights, and autonomy. At the same time, participation is a strategic move to align technical development with a robustly discerned public interest, and to build the mechanisms and mobilised publics that can hold AI's developers and governance bodies accountable.

Most critically, this project addresses a practical gap. Meaningful public involvement is needed at every level, but participation can't happen everywhere at once. We need clear processes, practical tools, shared approaches, and common language so that efforts on the ground and efforts at scale align and multiply their impact. To underpin this all, we also need a robust understanding, grounded in lived experience, of the current state of CSO influence over AI governance, the barriers to effective agenda-setting, and their needs and enablers to overcome these barriers. Our project delivered on this need.

Our approach has already gathered support and resonance from academia, civil society, and global institutions, as we have started building a community of practice around a more robust framework for AI governance with a focus on civic voices and upholding human rights. The results of this project have been shared with UNESCO’s Global Civil Society Organizations and Academic Network on AI Ethics and Policy, presented at leading international conferences and events, including the Paris Conference on AI and Digital Ethics, the PAIRS: Participatory AI and Research Practice Symposium, the Vilnius University International Scientific Conference: Human Centric AI: Ethics, Regulation, and Safety, AI Dialogues, and informally shared at the 2025 UN AI for Good Summit. Including this project in the PAVE Casebook would further improve the visibility and potential uptake of these valuable insights and framework for systemic change.
